steps.observation: You have 30 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
Every evening at seven, Elias climbed the iron steps of the Marrow Point Lighthouse, his hand trailing the rusted rail like a man greeting an old friend. The sea below muttered against the black rocks, a conversation he’d listened to for forty years.

The lamp had once been his father’s responsibility, and his grandfather’s before that. It was simple work now: flip the switches, check the backup generator, log the weather, send the report on a blinking console that rarely answered back. Satellite beacons and GPS had made men like him unnecessary on paper. But ships still called on the radio when the fog rolled in thick as wool, and they still said, “Good to hear your voice, Marrow Point.”

Tonight the fog was already pressing against the glass, impatient fingers smearing out the horizon. Elias lit the main lamp, watched it flare and steady, the great lens turning with a slow, patient grace. The beam swept the gray, a pale sword slicing nothingness.

He poured coffee from the dented pot and sat by the window, as he always did, and listened for what no one else believed in anymore: the bell.

On storm nights, when he was a boy, his father would pause halfway up the tower and hush him. “Listen,” he’d say, eyes narrowed at the sea, “you can hear the lost ones. They ring the bell when they pass.”

Elias had never heard anything but the wind and the sea. But he pretended he did, to please the old man, nodding solemnly as if distant chimes were drifting through the rain.

Years later, long after his father’s boots no longer creaked on the steps, after his own hair had turned the color of salt, Elias sat alone and listened. Most nights, there was only silence.

Tonight, however, the foghorn sounded once, low and mournful, then stuttered and died. The tower hummed uneasily. Power flickered. The console on the desk coughed out static.

Elias stood, heartbeat drumming in his ears. Backup systems whirred as the main current failed. The lamp dimmed, brightened, then steadied on the generator’s strained power. He knew the numbers: they had hours, maybe less, if the storm brewing beyond the fog turned ugly.

He climbed again, slower this time, feeling the tower sway. At the top, he checked every gauge, every fuse. The storm arrived as a sudden violence—rain slashed the glass, wind hurled itself at the lantern room. The world beyond the light vanished entirely.

And through that white roar, he heard it.

A faint, clear note, like metal struck in the deep. Then another. A gentle, sorrowful chiming, too regular to be wind, too high to be machinery.

The old bell, he thought hazily. The one they’d hauled up from a wreck decades before and mounted on the reef, where the waves could work it. It had rusted away years ago, finally torn loose by a winter gale. There was nothing left to ring.

Yet the sound came again—far, soft, insistent.

Elias leaned into the glass, the beam washing over the fog. “You’re hearing things,” he muttered. “Storm playing tricks.”

Then the radio crackled to life downstairs, a burst of panic punching through the static. He half-ran, half-slid down the stairs.

“—row Point, this is the trawler Hesper—repeat, this is Hesper—visibility zero, instruments are gone, we’re reading rocks dead ahead. Can you see us? Can anyone see us?”

Their voice was too close.

Elias grabbed the mic. “Hesper, this is Marrow Point. I’ve got you. Hold your heading if you can. You’re near the shoals. Can you hear the horn?”

“The horn’s dead,” the voice came back, brittle with fear. “We got nothing but your light, and it’s vanishing in this fog.”

As if to prove it, the generator groaned. The lamp flickered.

Elias looked at the panel—fuel dropping faster than it should. Something was wrong. The wind howled around the tower like a living thing.

The bell chimed again, clean and insistent, cutting through his thoughts.

He closed his eyes a moment, the mic cool in his hand. “All right, then,” he whispered to the storm. “Let’s do this the old way.”

He dashed into the storage room and hauled out the emergency lanterns: bulky, ancient things, their casings dulled with age. One by one he lit them, the flames catching reluctantly. He carried them up, breath burning, and set them in the windows of the watch room below the lantern, each wick turned high until their combined glow made a ragged crown beneath the main beam.

The radio crackled again. “Marrow Point, we’re drifting. We can’t see your light anymore.”

“Look lower,” Elias said hoarsely. “Look for the smaller lights. Steady on your current heading for two minutes, then turn ten degrees starboard. Do you hear me? Ten degrees. Do not overcorrect. Follow the line of the lights.”

Another chime, closer now, like a bell swinging slow in heavy water.

He watched the fog, saw nothing, and watched anyway. The generator’s hum faltered. The main lamp dimmed, its beam shrinking like a closing eye.

But the ring of the unseen bell hung in the air, now in front of the shoals, now to the east, as if marking a safe channel no map had ever known. Without thinking, Elias adjusted.

“Hesper, change that—fifteen degrees starboard, and slow your engines. There’s a current pulling you. Trust me.”

“Copy,” came the reply, shaky. “Fifteen degrees. Slowing. Still can’t see you.”

“You will,” he said. “In a moment.”

The bell pealed again, louder, nearer, then faded, as if retreating seaward. Rain rattled like thrown gravel. The tower trembled.

Minutes stretched thin. Elias felt each one like a weight in his chest.

Then, out of the milk-white dark, a shape emerged: first a smudge, then the faint rise of a bow cutting across the swell. The Hesper’s running lights winked into existence, smeared by rain.

“You’re clear of the shoals,” Elias said, the relief in his voice surprising him. “Maintain that course for half a mile, then resume your plotted heading.”

The reply was almost a laugh. “We’ve got you now. Thought we were finished. Thank you, Marrow Point. Didn’t think anyone still kept watch out here.”

Elias looked at the dimming lamp above his head, the wavering halos of the oil lanterns, the empty place where the old bell used to stand against the sky. The chiming had stopped. Only wind and water remained.

“That’s what we’re here for,” he said simply. “Safe passage.”

By the time the generator finally surrendered, the Hesper was a fading memory on the radar. The main lamp died, but the storm was already moving on, dragging the worst of itself northward. Dawn, pale and exhausted, began staining the fog.

Elias climbed to the lantern room one last time that night—more out of habit than necessity—and pressed his palm to the glass. The sea below rolled, dark and indifferent, but quieter now. Gulls cried somewhere beyond the mist, impatient for morning.

He listened.

No bell. No ghostly chime. Just the soft, steady exhale of the ocean.

“That’s all right,” he murmured. “You’ve done enough.”

When the maintenance crew from the mainland arrived three days later to fix the power, they brought new orders: the Marrow Point Lighthouse would be fully automated by the end of the year. His position, they explained, would be retired. Technology had improved.

Elias signed the papers with a careful hand. They asked if he’d be all right, out here alone for a few more months.

“I won’t be alone,” he said.

They assumed he meant the radio traffic, the rare visits from the coast guard. They didn’t ask further.

On his final night as keeper, fog rolled in again, soft and familiar. The new systems hummed to themselves, lights pulsing, lenses turning without his touch. He sat in the watch room with a cup of coffee gone cold, watching the obedient sweep of the beam.

When midnight came, he climbed to the lantern room once more. Below, the sea shifted and sighed around the dark teeth of the shoals.

“If you’re still out there,” he said quietly into the glass, “this is the last night I’m the one who answers.”

For a long time, there was nothing.

Then, faint as first rain, a single chime drifted up from the fog. One clear note, hanging impossibly in the air.

Elias smiled, a small, private thing. “I know,” he said. “But somebody will always be watching. Light’s still here. That’s what matters.”

He turned from the window, leaving the lamp to its measured circles, the sea to its endless murmur, the unseen bell to whatever work it did in waters no chart could name.

The world might forget there was once a man up here, shoulders bent against the wind, ears straining for sounds others could not hear. But as long as the light turned and ships passed safely in the night, the sea would remember.

And out beyond the shoals, when the fog came in heavy and the compass needles trembled, sailors swore they could hear a bell, leading them through the dark—one last gift from an old keeper who had never stopped listening.
